docs.title: Diaspora Event Fabric Service
docs.text:
This repository holds the web service of the Diaspora Event Fabric. Users sign in with Globus. For each user, the service creates an IAM user and a namespace, the prefix of the user's Kafka topic names. It creates the user's topics in that namespace on an Amazon MSK cluster, and offers REST routes to manage them and to consume records from the topics. It is a FastAPI application that runs as one container on AWS Lightsail and keeps its records in DynamoDB.

Our goal in the Diaspora project is to develop new methods for building next-generation resilient scientific applications capable of executing in an increasingly integrated research infrastructure.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• Documentation: how the service works, and how to run, test, deploy and operate it.

  • Diaspora Event SDK: the Python SDK for the Diaspora Event Fabric.

  • Security policy: how to report a vulnerability.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: For questions or contributions, contact the Diaspora Event Fabric team through the repository's issue tracker. Report a vulnerability privately, as the security policy says, and not in an issue. To change the code or the docs, read the contributing guide.

docs.title: Running locally
docs.text: This page runs the service on your machine, from a virtual environment or in a Docker container. The service reads its configuration from the environment variables at the end of this page; Deployment describes how the production container sets them.

docs.title: What a local run changes
docs.text:
With real AWS keys, a local run changes the production account

The service has no local or mock mode. It acts on the AWS account that its keys belong to, and on the MSK cluster that DEFAULT_SERVERS names:

  • IAM: POST /api/v3/user and POST /api/v3/key create IAM users, policies and access keys, and the DELETE routes delete them. When the service's keys table holds no key for the caller, POST /api/v3/key deletes every access key the caller's IAM user holds before it creates a new one. No variable changes where the IAM users go.
  • DynamoDB: without KEYS_TABLE_NAME, USERS_TABLE_NAME and NAMESPACE_TABLE_NAME, the service reads and writes the production tables.
  • MSK: with DEFAULT_SERVERS set, the topic routes create and delete topics on that cluster, and the consumer routes read from it.

IAM users and namespaces are named after the caller's Globus identity. If you call a local service with the Globus identity you use with the production service, it acts on the same IAM user as production and, with DEFAULT_SERVERS set, on the same topics.

docs.title: Keep a local run away from production data
docs.text:
The test tables keep the service's records out of the production tables, but they do not isolate IAM. IAM users, policies and access keys always go to the account that the AWS keys belong to, named after the caller's Globus identity.

  • Point the three tables at the test tables, which the live tests also use. .env.example does this:

    KEYS_TABLE_NAME=test-diaspora-keys-table
USERS_TABLE_NAME=test-diaspora-users-table
NAMESPACE_TABLE_NAME=test-diaspora-namespace-table

    If a table name is misspelt, the service creates a new table with that name in the account at its first write.

  • Leave DEFAULT_SERVERS unset unless you need the cluster. The topic routes then change only the service's records, and creating a consumer or recreating a topic fails with Kafka endpoint is not configured.

  • Call the service with a Globus identity that has no resources in the production service. By default the SDK requests tokens only for the production service's Globus client (Call the API). A local service that takes SDK tokens therefore runs with the production client, and the SDK signs you in with your own Globus identity, the one production also knows.
  • When you are done, and only for an identity that has no resources in production, call DELETE /api/v3/user. It deletes the IAM user, its policy, its access keys, its default namespace and that namespace's topics. For an identity you also use with production, it deletes the production IAM user and policy.

If you call a local service on the test tables with an identity that has a key in production, your first POST /api/v3/key finds no key in the test keys table. It deletes the access keys of your production IAM user and creates a new one. Clients that hold your old key, such as the SDK on your machine, can no longer connect to the cluster. The production keys table still holds the deleted key, and the production service's POST /api/v3/key keeps returning it with fresh set to false. To recover, call DELETE /api/v3/key on the production service, then POST /api/v3/key there: the first deletes the IAM user's keys and the stored key, and the second creates and stores a new one. After that, a local DELETE /api/v3/key or DELETE /api/v3/user with that identity still acts on the production IAM user, whatever the test tables hold. A local POST /api/v3/key keeps returning the deleted key from the test keys table. No route removes that item without also deleting the IAM user's keys, so delete it from the table directly.

To check only that the service starts, run it with the placeholder values of the unit tests (Run the unit tests locally). It makes no AWS call and serves its API documentation at /. API requests with a well-formed token reach Globus but not AWS, and fail: Globus rejects the placeholder client credentials, so they get 500 (Authentication lists the other answers).

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
The service needs Python 3.10 to 3.14. CI runs 3.14, and the container image runs 3.11. A full local run also needs AWS keys for the service's account and the ID and secret of the service's Globus confidential client. Without them, you can run the unit tests and start the service with placeholders.

python -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
cp .env.example .env

The required values are keys for the production service's AWS account and the production service's Globus client, so read What a local run changes before you fill them in. Fill in the required values in .env, which git ignores. Write each value without quotes and without a trailing comment: docker run --env-file takes every value literally.

docs.title: Run from the virtual environment
docs.text:
In development mode, with reloading on code changes:

(set -a; . ./.env; set +a; exec uvicorn web_service.main:app --port 8000 --reload)

As the container runs it, with gunicorn and one Uvicorn worker:

(set -a; . ./.env; set +a; exec gunicorn --bind 127.0.0.1:8000 -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker web_service.main:app)

The parentheses run each command in a subshell, so the values from .env stay out of your shell. Run one worker only: the service keeps consumer instances in the worker's memory (One worker). gunicorn reads its worker count from WEB_CONCURRENCY and extra options from GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS, so a value of either in your shell can change the number of workers.

The API documentation is at http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

docs.title: Run in Docker
docs.text:
Build the image from the repository root, then run it with .env:

docker build -t diaspora-service -f web_service/Dockerfile .
docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 --env-file .env diaspora-service

The Dockerfile pins the platform linux/amd64, which Lightsail runs.

docs.title: Call the API
docs.text: Every API route needs two headers: subject, the caller's Globus identity ID, and authorization, a Globus bearer token. The service accepts a token only when it names SERVER_CLIENT_ID in its audience and carries the scope https://auth.globus.org/scopes/<SERVER_CLIENT_ID>/action_all. The API reference shows how to get both headers with the Diaspora Event SDK. By default the SDK requests tokens for the production service's Globus client, so its tokens work with a local service only when SERVER_CLIENT_ID is that client's ID.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
The service checks the required variables when web_service.main is imported. A missing or empty one stops it with AssertionError: <NAME> environment variable is not set.

Variable Required Default What it does AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID yes The AWS access key the service uses for IAM, DynamoDB and MSK. AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY yes The secret of that key. SERVER_CLIENT_ID yes The ID of the Globus confidential client that tokens must be issued for. SERVER_SECRET yes The secret of that client, used to introspect tokens. AWS_ACCOUNT_ID yes The account in the ARNs of the IAM policies the service writes. AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION yes The region of the DynamoDB tables and the MSK cluster. MSK_CLUSTER_NAME yes The cluster named in those IAM policies. DEFAULT_SERVERS no unset The MSK bootstrap brokers for IAM authentication, as comma-separated host:port pairs. The service returns it to users with their key. Unset, the service makes no Kafka calls. KEYS_TABLE_NAME no diaspora-keys-table The DynamoDB table of access keys. USERS_TABLE_NAME no diaspora-users-table The DynamoDB table of the namespaces each user owns. NAMESPACE_TABLE_NAME no diaspora-namespace-table The DynamoDB table of the topics in each namespace. MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE no 50 The most topics a namespace may hold. A value that is not a whole number of at least 1 is logged and replaced by 50. CONSUMER_INSTANCE_TIMEOUT_MS no 300000 (5 minutes) How long a consumer instance may sit idle before the service closes it. A value that is not an integer, including an empty one, stops the service at start with a ValueError. IAM_USER_PERMISSIONS_BOUNDARY_ARN no unset The ARN of a managed policy that the service sets as the permissions boundary of every IAM user it creates. Production leaves it unset; the live tests set it (Testing).

The AWS SDK reads the two key variables itself, and with them AWS_SESSION_TOKEN when you use temporary credentials.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The tests come in two sets:

  • Unit tests: every test not marked integration. They mock or stub AWS and Kafka and need no account, credentials or network. Any of them that opens a network connection fails.
  • Live tests: the tests marked integration. They create real IAM users, DynamoDB items and Kafka topics in the AWS account and on the MSK cluster that the credentials point to, and delete them afterwards. Every test in db_service_test.py, iam_service_test.py, kafka_service_test.py, namespace_service_test.py and web_service_test.py is marked integration by tests/conftest.py; other files mark their live tests one by one.

docs.title: Run the unit tests locally
docs.text:
Install the dev extras first (pip install -e ".[dev]", as in Running locally). The service checks a few environment variables at import, so give it placeholders, and point the AWS SDK away from any credentials you have:

AWS_CONFIG_FILE=/dev/null \
AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=/dev/null \
AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true \
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=dummy-not-real \
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=dummy-not-real \
SERVER_CLIENT_ID=00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 \
SERVER_SECRET=dummy-not-real \
AWS_ACCOUNT_ID=000000000000 \
AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION=us-east-1 \
MSK_CLUSTER_NAME=dummy \
pytest tests/ -m "not integration"

docs.title: Run the live tests locally
docs.text:
The live tests need the service's environment variables with real values (AWS keys, AWS_ACCOUNT_ID, AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION, MSK_CLUSTER_NAME, DEFAULT_SERVERS and the Globus client settings):

pytest tests/ -m integration -vv -s

They write to the account and the cluster the credentials point to. Do not run them while another live run is in progress: some tests assert on records shared by all runs. With the live tests' own keys (see below), also set IAM_USER_PERMISSIONS_BOUNDARY_ARN to the boundary policy's ARN, or every test that creates an IAM user is denied.

Their DynamoDB items go to the test-diaspora-* tables. Most live tests name those tables in code, but the live tests in consumer_service_test.py take the tables from KEYS_TABLE_NAME, USERS_TABLE_NAME and NAMESPACE_TABLE_NAME when these are set. Leave them unset, or set them to the test tables as tests.yml does, so that no test writes to the production tables.

With coverage, over both sets:

coverage erase
coverage run -m pytest tests/
coverage report

docs.title: What runs in CI
docs.text:
Workflow Job Tests When Secrets tests.yml unit unit pull requests; pushes to main, test-me-* and tags; nightly; manual dispatch none tests.yml live live, then the sweep (nightly only) pushes to main, nightly, manual dispatch the live tests' AWS keys, or the service's while those are not set deployment.yml unit unit before every deploy none
  • The deploy job in deployment.yml waits for its unit job, so a failing unit test on main stops the deploy.
  • The live job never runs on pull requests, tag pushes or test-me-* pushes. A manual dispatch runs the live tests of the branch it is dispatched on, whichever branch that is.
  • live runs in the live-tests concurrency group, so no two live runs happen at the same time. GitHub keeps only one pending run per group: a run that is waiting can be cancelled by a newer one.
  • In the nightly run, after the live tests whether they passed or failed (not when the job was cancelled), the last step of live runs scripts/sweep_test_resources.py --apply. It deletes what earlier live runs left behind: IAM users and policies named test-subject-test<8 hex> older than two hours, and Kafka topics named test-namespace-<16 hex>.test-topic-<16 hex> or ns-test<8 hex>.test-topic-<suffix> (with the suffixes the tests use) whose namespace the service has no record of and that is not the default namespace of another IAM user. It also selects leftovers with the names the tests used before (test-subject-<16 hex>, ns-<12 hex>.test-topic-<suffix>). The live tests' own identity can delete IAM users and policies with those names, but it cannot see or delete topics with those names; only the service's keys can (see Create the identity). Kafka keeps no creation time for topics, so topics are not filtered by age: a local live run around the nightly time can lose its topics. Without --apply the script only lists what it would delete.

docs.title: The live tests' AWS identity
docs.text:
The live tests and the sweep run against the service's production account and MSK cluster, as an IAM user of their own whose policy lets them touch only what they create. Its keys are the repository secrets LIVE_TESTS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and LIVE_TESTS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; while either of them is not set, live uses the service's keys.

The policy, tests/live_identity/identity-policy.json, allows:

  • Creating IAM users under /msk-users/ and managed policies under /msk-policy/ whose names are test-subject-test followed by exactly 8 characters, attaching such a policy to such a user, and creating access keys for such a user. A user can be created, or given a policy, only with the boundary below as its permissions boundary.
  • Reading any IAM user named test-subject-*, detaching its policies, deleting its access keys and deleting it, and deleting any policy of that name, so the sweep also removes test users named the way the tests used to name them.
  • Listing all IAM users and policies, which the sweep needs.
  • Reading and writing items in the three test-diaspora-* tables.
  • In the service's own tables, reading only the global namespace list and the records of test namespaces. Nothing else in them, and never the keys table.
  • On the cluster: connecting; creating, reading, writing and deleting topics in namespaces starting ns-test or test-namespace-; and using consumer groups in namespaces starting ns-test.

Every IAM user the tests create gets the permissions boundary tests/live_identity/boundary-policy.json, so whatever policy is attached to it, the user can do no more than read and write test topics and groups. The service sets that boundary when IAM_USER_PERMISSIONS_BOUNDARY_ARN is set, and sets none when it is not.

docs.title: Naming live-test resources
docs.text:
The identity can touch only resources with these names, and the sweep finds only these, so every live test takes its names from tests/live_identity:

  • a subject (and so an IAM user and policy): live_subject(), which returns test-subject-test<8 hex>; the shared random_subject fixture in tests/conftest.py returns one. Its default namespace is ns-test<8 hex>.
  • a namespace without a user: live_namespace(), which returns ns-test<8 hex>.
  • Kafka topics and consumer groups: <namespace>.<name> in one of those namespaces, or in test-namespace-<hex>.

A real user's subject is a UUID, so its default namespace is ns- and 12 hex digits, which never starts with ns-test.

docs.title: Create the identity
docs.text:
Run these with an administrator's credentials, at a time when no live run is in progress.

First create the boundary, the identity's policy, the user and its access key. Fill in the account ID, region, MSK cluster name and the cluster's UUID (the last part of its ARN, from aws kafka list-clusters-v2):

ACCOUNT_ID=<account-id>
REGION=<region>
CLUSTER_NAME=<cluster-name>
CLUSTER_UUID=<cluster-uuid>

render() {
  sed -e "s/<account-id>/$ACCOUNT_ID/g" -e "s/<region>/$REGION/g" \
    -e "s/<cluster-name>/$CLUSTER_NAME/g" \
    -e "s/<cluster-uuid>/$CLUSTER_UUID/g" "$1"
}

aws iam create-policy --path /diaspora-test/ \
  --policy-name test-user-boundary \
  --policy-document "$(render tests/live_identity/boundary-policy.json)"
aws iam create-policy --path /diaspora-test/ \
  --policy-name diaspora-live-tests \
  --policy-document "$(render tests/live_identity/identity-policy.json)"
aws iam create-user --user-name diaspora-live-tests
aws iam attach-user-policy --user-name diaspora-live-tests \
  --policy-arn "arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:policy/diaspora-test/diaspora-live-tests"
aws iam create-access-key --user-name diaspora-live-tests

Do not name the user test-subject-*, or its policy would let it manage itself.

Just before storing the key, delete with the service's keys everything earlier live runs left behind, whatever its age. Until the secrets are set, live runs use the service's keys and create test users without a boundary, and the identity cannot see or delete the topics named the way the tests used to name them. The sweep reads the region and the bootstrap servers from AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION and DEFAULT_SERVERS. Without --apply it lists what it would delete:

python scripts/sweep_test_resources.py --min-age-hours 0
python scripts/sweep_test_resources.py --apply --min-age-hours 0

Then store the key's AccessKeyId and SecretAccessKey as the repository secrets. Each command prompts for the value, which keeps the key out of the shell history:

gh secret set LIVE_TESTS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID --repo haochenpan/diaspora-service
gh secret set LIVE_TESTS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY --repo haochenpan/diaspora-service

Once both secrets are set, live runs as the identity and sets IAM_USER_PERMISSIONS_BOUNDARY_ARN to arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:policy/diaspora-test/test-user-boundary.

To change what the identity may do, edit the template and apply it as a new default version of the policy. IAM keeps at most five versions of a policy, so when it holds five, first delete the oldest version that is not the default, replacing v1 below with the ID the list prints with the earliest date:

POLICY_ARN="arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:policy/diaspora-test/diaspora-live-tests"
aws iam list-policy-versions --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" \
  --query 'Versions[?!IsDefaultVersion].[VersionId,CreateDate]' --output text
aws iam delete-policy-version --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" --version-id v1
aws iam create-policy-version --set-as-default --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" \
  --policy-document "$(render tests/live_identity/identity-policy.json)"

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
The service runs as one container on the AWS Lightsail container service diaspora-web-service in us-east-1. The deployment workflow (.github/workflows/deployment.yml) builds the image from web_service/Dockerfile and deploys it. Parts of the workflow are adapted from fdiesel/github-action-deploy-aws-lightsail-container. Rollback, logs, triage and credential rotation are in the runbook.

In this page a deploy is one run of the workflow, and a deployment is what Lightsail runs: a numbered version that names the container, its image and its environment.

docs.title: What triggers a deploy
docs.text:
• A push to main, which includes merging a pull request. A push whose changed files are all under docs/, are Markdown files, or are mkdocs.yml does not deploy; a push that changes code and docs together does.
  • A manual run of the workflow (see Deploy by hand).

Nothing else deploys: not pull requests, other branches, tags or a schedule.

Deploys run one at a time in the production concurrency group. A deploy in progress is never cancelled. While one runs, GitHub keeps only the newest waiting run and cancels older waiting runs. After several quick merges, the running deploy finishes, and then the newest waiting run deploys the latest main.

docs.title: What the workflow does
docs.text:
1. The unit job runs the unit tests (the reusable unit-tests.yml workflow, without secrets; see Testing). If a test fails, nothing is deployed.
  2. The deploy-lightsail-containers job then runs these steps:
    1. It configures AWS credentials from the AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY repository secrets for us-east-1, and checks them with aws sts get-caller-identity.
    2. It installs the Lightsail CLI plugin (lightsailctl), which aws lightsail push-container-image needs.
    3. It checks out the commit and builds the image from web_service/Dockerfile, tagged docker.
    4. It creates the container service with power micro (0.25 vCPU, 1 GB of memory) and scale 1. When the service already exists, this step fails and the job continues.
    5. It pushes the image with the label docker. Lightsail stores it as :diaspora-web-service.docker.<N>, where <N> grows by one with each push.
    6. It creates a deployment with one container named flask that runs the new image, listens on port 8000 over HTTP and is the public endpoint. The container's environment comes from the DOCKER_* secrets (Secrets). Each deployment carries its whole environment, so a variable the workflow does not pass is unset in the container.
    7. It waits for the deployment to become active (The wait step).
    8. It deletes the stored images that no deployment still needs. It keeps the images of the active deployment, of any deployment still activating, and of the most recent inactive deployment, which is the rollback target. This step runs only after the wait step succeeds, and an error in it does not fail the run.

docs.title: The wait step
docs.text:
The step reads the version number of the new deployment, then checks the service every 30 seconds. It succeeds when that version is the current deployment and its state is ACTIVE. While a new deployment activates, Lightsail keeps the previous one serving; if the new one fails, the previous one stays active.

Error in the run log What it usually means What to do No pending deployment found for diaspora-web-service Right after the create call, Lightsail showed no pending deployment. Check the service's state (Check a deploy) and the previous step's log. Deployment <version> failed; check the container logs Lightsail marked the deployment FAILED: the container did not start, or did not pass Lightsail's health check, which requests /. A missing environment variable is one cause. Read the container log and triage the failure. Deployment <version> is no longer pending and did not become active The version is neither current nor pending. Another deployment, made from the console or the CLI while the workflow waited, can replace it; workflow runs do not overlap, so it was not another run. List the deployments and their states (Roll back a deploy shows the command). Deployment <version> is not active after 20 minutes Lightsail was still activating the deployment when the step stopped waiting. It can still become active or fail. Check the service's state and the container log. The image cleanup did not run.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
The deploy uses two sets of repository secrets. AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY are the workflow's own AWS key. It needs access to the Lightsail container service only, and the container never sees it. The DOCKER_* secrets become the container's environment, without the prefix. The live job of tests.yml, whose last step is the nightly sweep, reads the same DOCKER_* secrets (the AWS key only while the live tests' own key is not set), so a change to one of them also reaches the live tests.

Secret Container variable Notes AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID none The deploy's AWS access key ID. AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY none The deploy's AWS secret access key. DOCKER_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID Required. DOCKER_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY Required. DOCKER_SERVER_CLIENT_ID SERVER_CLIENT_ID Required. DOCKER_SERVER_SECRET SERVER_SECRET Required. DOCKER_AWS_ACCOUNT_ID AWS_ACCOUNT_ID Required. DOCKER_AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION Required. DOCKER_MSK_CLUSTER_NAME MSK_CLUSTER_NAME Required. DOCKER_DEFAULT_SERVERS DEFAULT_SERVERS Needed for any Kafka call. DOCKER_CLIENT_ID CLIENT_ID Unused by the service. tests.yml runs the live tests only when this secret is set, so runs without the repository's secrets skip them. DOCKER_CLIENT_SECRET CLIENT_SECRET Unused. DOCKER_CLIENT_SCOPE CLIENT_SCOPE Unused. DOCKER_MSK_CLUSTER_ARN_SUFFIX MSK_CLUSTER_ARN_SUFFIX Unused.

docs.title: Container environment
docs.text:
The service checks seven variables when web_service.main is imported, which happens when the gunicorn worker starts. Each must be set and non-empty. A missing one stops the worker with AssertionError: <NAME> environment variable is not set., and Lightsail marks the deployment failed.

Variable Required Default What it sets AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID yes The AWS key the service uses for IAM, DynamoDB and MSK IAM authentication. AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY yes The secret of that key. SERVER_CLIENT_ID yes The ID of the service's Globus confidential client. Every token must name it in its audience and carry the scope https://auth.globus.org/scopes/<SERVER_CLIENT_ID>/action_all. SERVER_SECRET yes The secret of that client, used to introspect tokens. AWS_ACCOUNT_ID yes The account in the ARNs of the IAM policies the service writes. AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION yes The region of the DynamoDB tables and the MSK cluster. MSK_CLUSTER_NAME yes The cluster named in those IAM policies. DEFAULT_SERVERS no none The MSK bootstrap brokers for IAM authentication, as comma-separated host:port pairs. Without it the service starts, but topic creates and deletes change only the service's own records and not the cluster, and topic recreates and consumer creates fail with Kafka endpoint is not configured. KEYS_TABLE_NAME no diaspora-keys-table The DynamoDB table of access keys. USERS_TABLE_NAME no diaspora-users-table The DynamoDB table of users. NAMESPACE_TABLE_NAME no diaspora-namespace-table The DynamoDB table of namespaces. MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE no 50 The most topics a namespace may hold. A value that is not a whole number of at least 1 is logged and replaced by 50. CONSUMER_INSTANCE_TIMEOUT_MS no 300000 (5 minutes) How long a consumer instance may sit idle before the service closes it. The service looks for idle instances every 30 seconds. A value that is not an integer stops the worker at start with a ValueError. IAM_USER_PERMISSIONS_BOUNDARY_ARN no none The ARN of a managed policy that the service sets as the permissions boundary of every IAM user it creates; unset or empty, it sets none. Production leaves it unset. The live tests set it (The live tests' AWS identity).

The workflow passes none of the optional variables, so production runs with their defaults. To set one, add it to the environment block in deployment.yml.

docs.title: One worker
docs.text:
The Dockerfile starts gunicorn without --workers, so it runs one Uvicorn worker, and the service runs at scale 1. Consumer instances live in that one process's memory, so the service must stay at one worker on one node. With a second worker or node, a request can reach a process that does not hold its instance and gets 404 with error code 40403 (Consumer instance not found). Do not pass --workers to gunicorn, do not set WEB_CONCURRENCY (gunicorn reads its worker count from it) or GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS (gunicorn reads extra options from it), and keep the scale at 1.

Every deploy or restart stops the process and drops every consumer instance. Clients then get 40403 and must create a new instance. A new instance in the same consumer group starts from the offsets the group last committed to Kafka.

docs.title: From GitHub
docs.text:
gh workflow run deployment.yml --ref main
gh run list --workflow deployment.yml --event workflow_dispatch --limit 1   # the run's ID
gh run watch <run-id>

A manual run goes through the same unit tests, queue, wait step and cleanup as a push. It deploys the branch named by --ref; a run on another branch is replaced by the next deploy of main.

docs.title: From your machine
docs.text:
Use this only when GitHub Actions cannot run the workflow. It skips the unit tests, the wait step and the image cleanup. You need Docker, the AWS CLI with the Lightsail container services plugin, jq, and AWS credentials with the deploy's Lightsail access.

The steps copy the current deployment's container, environment included, and change only its image, so they need no secret values. If the container service does not exist, create it before step 1:

aws lightsail create-container-service --region us-east-1 \
    --service-name diaspora-web-service --power micro --scale 1

A new service has no deployment to copy, so step 3 must then set the environment by hand (Set the environment by hand). Its public URL is also likely to change: AWS builds a service's default domain from a randomly generated identifier of the service, and clients and these docs use the current domain.

  1. Build the image from the repository root. The Dockerfile pins linux/amd64, the platform Lightsail runs.

    docker build -t docker -f web_service/Dockerfile .

  2. Push it and keep the name Lightsail gives it:

    output=$(aws lightsail push-container-image --region us-east-1 \
    --service-name diaspora-web-service --label docker --image docker)
image=$(echo "$output" | sed -n 's/.*Refer to this image as "\(.*\)" in deployments.*/\1/p')
echo "$image"   # for example :diaspora-web-service.docker.<N>

  3. Copy the current deployment's container and set its image. $containers then holds the container's secrets, so do not print it.

    containers=$(aws lightsail get-container-services --region us-east-1 \
    --service-name diaspora-web-service \
    --query 'containerServices[0].currentDeployment.containers' --output json |
  jq --arg image "$image" '.flask.image = $image')
jq -e '.flask.environment' > /dev/null <<< "$containers" ||
  echo "No current deployment: set the environment by hand (below)."

  4. Create the deployment. The command prints the deployment with its environment, so the example discards its output.

    aws lightsail create-container-service-deployment --region us-east-1 \
    --service-name diaspora-web-service \
    --containers "$containers" \
    --public-endpoint '{"containerName": "flask", "containerPort": 8000}' > /dev/null

    Keep the container name flask: the public endpoint and the logs refer to it.

  5. Check the deploy.

docs.title: Set the environment by hand
docs.text:
To change a variable, or to deploy to a service with no current deployment, read the values into the shell first. read -rs keeps each value off the screen and out of shell history. The SVC_ prefix keeps the values apart from the AWS CLI's own credentials. A value set this way lasts only until the next workflow deploy, which rebuilds the environment from the DOCKER_* secrets and deployment.yml; update the matching secret, or for an optional variable deployment.yml, too.

for var in AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY SERVER_CLIENT_ID SERVER_SECRET \
    AWS_ACCOUNT_ID AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION MSK_CLUSTER_NAME DEFAULT_SERVERS; do
  printf '%s: ' "$var"; IFS= read -rs value; echo
  export "SVC_$var=$value"
done
unset value

To change one variable of the current deployment, run the loop with only that name (for var in MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE; do) and extend the filter of step 3, for example jq --arg image "$image" '.flask.image = $image | .flask.environment.MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE = env.SVC_MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE'. For a service with no current deployment, build the whole container instead of step 3:

containers=$(jq -n --arg image "$image" '{
  flask: {
    image: $image,
    ports: {"8000": "HTTP"},
    environment: {
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: env.SVC_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID,
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: env.SVC_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY,
      SERVER_CLIENT_ID: env.SVC_SERVER_CLIENT_ID,
      SERVER_SECRET: env.SVC_SERVER_SECRET,
      AWS_ACCOUNT_ID: env.SVC_AWS_ACCOUNT_ID,
      AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION: env.SVC_AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION,
      MSK_CLUSTER_NAME: env.SVC_MSK_CLUSTER_NAME,
      DEFAULT_SERVERS: env.SVC_DEFAULT_SERVERS
    }
  }
}')

After the deployment is created, remove the values from the shell with unset "${!SVC_@}" in bash or unset -m 'SVC_*' in zsh.

docs.title: Check a deploy
docs.text:
aws lightsail get-container-services --region us-east-1 \
    --service-name diaspora-web-service \
    --query 'containerServices[0].{state: state, current: currentDeployment.[version, state], image: currentDeployment.containers.flask.image, next: nextDeployment.[version, state]}'

A finished deploy shows the service RUNNING, the current deployment ACTIVE with the new image, and next as null. Keep the --query: without it, the command prints the container's environment, secrets included.

Then check that the service answers. It serves its API documentation at /, so this prints 200:

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: An operator can watch the Lightsail container service and the MSK brokers. Every command on this page only reads; the runbook says what to do when something looks wrong.

docs.title: The Lightsail service
docs.text:
The service runs on Lightsail's micro power (0.25 vCPU and 1 GB of memory), and Lightsail records its CPU and memory use as percentages of that. Each open consumer instance holds a Kafka consumer in the service's memory. The Lightsail console shows these metrics on the service's page. From the CLI, memory use in 5-minute periods:

aws lightsail get-container-service-metric-data --region us-east-1 \
    --service-name diaspora-web-service --metric-name MemoryUtilization \
    --start-time <start-time> --end-time <end-time> \
    --period 300 --statistics Average Maximum

The times are in ISO 8601, such as 2026-10-26T06:00:00Z. --metric-name CPUUtilization gives the CPU use. The history starts at the current deployment: AWS says that a new deployment makes the existing utilization metrics disappear, so every deploy, rollback or credential rotation clears them.

The container's log holds gunicorn's and the service's output for the last three days (Read the logs). aws lightsail get-container-services shows whether the service is running and which deployment is active (Check a deploy).

On GitHub Actions, the deployment workflow's runs show each deploy, and the tests workflow's runs show the live tests, which run nightly and on every push to main. The live tests run against the AWS account and the MSK cluster, not against the deployed service.

docs.title: The MSK brokers
docs.text: Each broker's CPUCreditBalance metric in CloudWatch (namespace AWS/Kafka, dimensions Cluster Name and Broker ID) is the number of CPU credits it has left. AWS says that running out "can have a negative impact on your cluster's performance" (Broker CPU credits).

docs.title: The Kafka console
docs.text: The Diaspora Admin Console is a Kafbat UI instance that shows the cluster's topics, consumer groups and consumer lag. Its statistics can be up to 5 minutes old.

docs.title: Runbook
docs.text: Tasks for operating the deployed service: rolling back, reading the logs, triaging a failed deploy, watching the brokers' CPU credits and rotating credentials. Deployment describes the workflow, the secrets and the container's environment that these tasks refer to. The Lightsail commands use the region us-east-1; angle brackets mark values to fill in.

docs.title: Roll back a deploy
docs.text:
Roll back when a deployment became active but the service misbehaves. A deployment that fails needs no rollback: Lightsail keeps the previous one active.

The workflow's image cleanup keeps the images of the active deployment, of any deployment still activating, and of the most recent inactive deployment. After a deploy, Lightsail therefore holds the current image and the one before it. To see the deployments and the stored images:

aws lightsail get-container-service-deployments --region us-east-1 \
    --service-name diaspora-web-service \
    --query 'deployments[].{version: version, state: state, image: containers.flask.image}' \
    --output table
aws lightsail get-container-images --region us-east-1 \
    --service-name diaspora-web-service --query 'containerImages[].image'

Lightsail lists up to 50 deployment versions, but only the versions whose image is still stored can be deployed again.

  1. Hold merges to main until step 4 lands. The next push to main deploys main, which would bring the bad change back.

  2. Deploy the previous image with the current environment, from the console or the CLI.

    • Console: in the Lightsail console, open Containers, then diaspora-web-service, then the Deployments tab. Choose Modify your deployment, then Choose stored image for flask, pick the previous image, and choose Save and deploy.
    • CLI: set image=':diaspora-web-service.docker.<N>', the previous image, then run steps 3 and 4 of Deploy from your machine. They copy the current deployment's environment and change only the image.

    Under Deployment versions, the actions menu (⋮) of an older version also has Create new deployment. It reuses that version's environment as well as its image, so a secret changed since then returns to its old value.

  3. Check the deploy.

  4. Revert the change on main, for example with git revert <commit> in a pull request. Merging the revert deploys main without the change.

To go back further than the stored previous image, revert on main and let the workflow build and deploy it.

docs.title: Read the logs
docs.text:
aws lightsail get-container-log returns one page of entries at a time, and the AWS CLI does not fetch the following pages for you. A call without --start-time can return an old page that misses the latest deployment. This loop prints every entry since start, page by page:

start='2026-10-26T07:00:00Z'   # the earliest time to read, in UTC
token=()
while :; do
  page=$(aws lightsail get-container-log --region us-east-1 \
      --service-name diaspora-web-service --container-name flask \
      --start-time "$start" "${token[@]}" --output json)
  jq -r '.logEvents[] | "\(.createdAt)\t\(.message)"' <<< "$page"
  next=$(jq -r '.nextPageToken // empty' <<< "$page")
  if [ -z "$next" ] || [ "$(jq '.logEvents | length' <<< "$page")" -eq 0 ]; then
    break
  fi
  token=(--page-token "$next")
done

Each page carries a nextPageToken; the loop passes it back with --page-token and stops at a page with no entries. Lightsail can return a token with the last page, so an empty page is the end. To keep only matching lines, add --filter-pattern, for example --filter-pattern AssertionError, and to end the period, --end-time.

The container is named flask in every deployment; docker is the image label, not the container name. The log holds what gunicorn and the service write to stdout and stderr. Lightsail keeps the last three days of log entries.

In the console, the Deployments tab has an Open log link for the current deployment's container. For an earlier or failed version, open the version's actions menu (⋮) under Deployment versions, choose Show details, then Open log.

docs.title: Triage a failed deploy
docs.text:
Find the failed step in the run on GitHub Actions.

Failed step Usual cause Fix unit A unit test fails on main. Nothing was deployed. Fix the test or the code on main. Configure AWS credentials or Verify AWS credential The deploy's key in the AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY secrets is wrong, deactivated or deleted. Update the secrets (Rotate an AWS access key). Install AWS Lightsail plugin The plugin's download failed, or its checksum did not match. Rerun the job; if the checksum still fails, check the pinned release in deployment.yml. Checkout code GitHub could not check out the commit. Rerun the job. Build Docker container for AWS Lightsail docker build failed; the step log shows the failing Dockerfile instruction. Reproduce it with docker build -f web_service/Dockerfile . and fix it on main. Idempotently create Lightsail container service This step's error is expected on every run: the service exists. The step does not fail the run. Nothing. Push Docker image to Lightsail and deploy An AWS CLI call failed; the step log shows its error. Fix the cause the error names, then deploy again. Wait for the deployment to become active The deployment failed or did not finish in time (The wait step). Read the container log, as below.

When a deployment fails, read the log around the time of the deploy. A worker that cannot start ends with gunicorn's Reason: Worker failed to boot., and the traceback above it names the cause:

  • AssertionError: <NAME> environment variable is not set. means the DOCKER_<NAME> secret is missing or empty. Set it with gh secret set DOCKER_<NAME>, then deploy again with gh workflow run deployment.yml --ref main.
  • ValueError: invalid literal for int() at start means CONSUMER_INSTANCE_TIMEOUT_MS is set to a value that is not an integer.

To reproduce a start-up failure locally, build and run the image as in Running.

docs.title: Broker CPU credits
docs.text:
The MSK cluster's brokers are burstable instances, kafka.t3.small as of October 2026 (see the Kafka console page). A burstable broker earns CPU credits at a fixed rate and spends them while it runs above its baseline. When the balance runs out, AWS's MSK metrics reference says only that this "can have a negative impact on your cluster's performance". In October 2026 the Kafka console's load spent one broker's credits, and topic creation and deletion stalled until the console's instance was stopped.

Each broker's balance is the CPUCreditBalance metric in CloudWatch, in the cluster's region (the AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION value). In the CloudWatch console, open Metrics, then All metrics, then AWS/Kafka, then Broker ID, Cluster Name, and select CPUCreditBalance for each broker. From the CLI, for one broker:

aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region <region> \
    --namespace AWS/Kafka --metric-name CPUCreditBalance \
    --dimensions Name="Cluster Name",Value=<cluster-name> Name="Broker ID",Value=<broker-id> \
    --start-time <start-time> --end-time <end-time> \
    --period 3600 --statistics Minimum

<cluster-name> is the MSK_CLUSTER_NAME value, the broker IDs start at 1, and the times are in ISO 8601, such as 2026-10-25T00:00:00Z.

If a balance keeps falling, find the load that spends it. The Kafka console's statistics refresh is one known source; its page says to stop the console's instance in that case.

docs.title: Rotate credentials
docs.text:
The deploy and the service use three credentials, each stored in GitHub secrets:

Credential Secrets Also used by The deploy's AWS key, used by the workflow AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY The container's AWS key, used by the service DOCKER_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, DOCKER_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY The live job of tests.yml and its nightly sweep, while the live tests' own key is not set The Globus confidential client's secret, used by the service DOCKER_SERVER_SECRET The live job of tests.yml

The running container keeps the values it started with. A new value reaches it only through a new deployment, and the workflow builds each deployment's environment from the secrets as they are at that run. Every such deploy restarts the service and drops its consumer instances, whose clients then get 40403 (One worker).

docs.title: Rotate an AWS access key
docs.text:
An IAM user can hold two access keys at once, so the old key keeps working until you deactivate it. The deploy's key and the container's key may belong to the same IAM user; check before you delete either.

  1. Find the IAM user the key belongs to, and list its keys: aws iam list-access-keys --user-name <user>. If it already has two, run aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id <key-id> on each. Its ServiceName says which credential the key is: the deploy's key was last used by Lightsail or STS, the container's by IAM, DynamoDB or Kafka. Delete only a key with no recent use.
  2. Create a key: aws iam create-access-key --user-name <user>. The output is the only time AWS shows the secret.
  3. Update the matching secrets from the table, for example gh secret set DOCKER_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and gh secret set DOCKER_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; each prompts for its value.
  4. Deploy: gh workflow run deployment.yml --ref main. A new deploy key is checked by the run's Verify AWS credential step. For a new container key, check the deploy and read the log for AWS errors.
  5. Check when the old key was last used: aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id <old-key-id>. A use after the new deployment became active means something still holds the old key. Anything else that holds it, such as a local file you source for the live tests, needs the new key too.
  6. Deactivate the old key: aws iam update-access-key --user-name <user> --access-key-id <old-key-id> --status Inactive. When nothing has failed with the old key inactive, delete it with aws iam delete-access-key --user-name <user> --access-key-id <old-key-id>.

docs.title: Rotate the Globus client secret
docs.text:
1. In Globus developer settings, open the confidential client whose client ID is the SERVER_CLIENT_ID value, and add a client secret. Globus shows it only once.
  2. Update the secret: gh secret set DOCKER_SERVER_SECRET.
  3. Deploy: gh workflow run deployment.yml --ref main, then check the deploy and make one authenticated call, such as GET /api/v3/namespace (API Reference shows how to get a token).
  4. Delete the old secret in the Globus developer settings.

Keep the client itself. Its ID is part of the scope every token must carry (https://auth.globus.org/scopes/<SERVER_CLIENT_ID>/action_all), so a new client would make the service reject every token issued for the old one.

docs.title: Acknowledgments
docs.text: This project's layout and workflows are primarily based on Greg's Python template.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The service is one FastAPI application, web_service.main:app, that runs in one process. It authenticates each caller with Globus, then acts for that caller with its own AWS key: it manages the caller's IAM user, keeps the caller's records in three DynamoDB tables, and creates, deletes and reads topics on one Amazon MSK cluster.

docs.title: The request path
docs.text:
1. A client sends an HTTPS request to the public endpoint of the Lightsail container service. Lightsail forwards it over HTTP to port 8000 of the one container, which deployment.yml names flask (Deployment).
  2. In the container, gunicorn runs one Uvicorn worker, which serves the FastAPI application. web_service/main.py builds the application and its routes in the class DiasporaService.
  3. The route handler checks the caller's token with Globus (Authentication).
  4. The handler calls the service classes in web_service/services.py:
    • WebService runs each user, key and topic operation across the classes below.
    • IAMService creates and deletes IAM users, their policies and their access keys.
    • NamespaceService checks namespace and topic names and keeps the namespace and topic records, through DynamoDBService.
    • DynamoDBService reads and writes the three tables.
    • KafkaService creates and deletes topics with a Kafka admin client.
  5. The consumer routes call ConsumerService in web_service/consumer_service.py, which keeps Kafka consumers in memory (State in memory).

Calls to Globus, IAM, DynamoDB and Kafka block, so the handlers run them in FastAPI's thread pool. On the event loop, they would stall every other request.

The service reaches AWS with the key in AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Its Kafka clients connect to the brokers in DEFAULT_SERVERS over SASL_SSL with the OAUTHBEARER mechanism, using tokens that aws-msk-iam-sasl-signer-python signs with that key for the region in AWS_ACCOUNT_REGION. The service does not use the users' IAM keys for its own calls.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Every API route takes two headers: subject, the caller's Globus identity ID, and authorization, Bearer followed by a Globus access token. The class AuthManager in web_service/utils.py checks them in this order:

  1. subject is a UUID.
  2. The token has the Bearer prefix, is 33 to 254 characters long, and holds only letters, digits and underscores.
  3. Globus token introspection, called with the service's confidential client (SERVER_CLIENT_ID and SERVER_SECRET), reports the token active.
  4. The token's sub is the subject header.
  5. The token's audience includes SERVER_CLIENT_ID.
  6. The token's scopes include https://auth.globus.org/scopes/<SERVER_CLIENT_ID>/action_all.

A request missing one of the headers gets FastAPI's 422. A failed check ends the request: the user, key, namespace and topic routes answer 200 with {"status": "error", "reason": ...}, and the consumer routes answer 401. Step 3 fails this way only when Globus answers that the token is inactive. When the introspection call itself fails, for example because Globus rejects SERVER_CLIENT_ID and SERVER_SECRET, the Globus SDK raises an AuthAPIError that the service does not catch, and the route answers 500. After the checks, the service trusts subject as the caller's identity and names the caller's resources after it.

docs.title: Each user's resources
docs.text:
A namespace is the prefix of the Kafka names of a user's topics and consumer groups. Each user gets one, the default namespace, when the service creates the user.

Resource Name Created by Deleted by IAM user the subject, under the path /msk-users/ POST /api/v3/user, or POST /api/v3/key when the keys table holds no key for the user DELETE /api/v3/user IAM managed policy, attached to the user the subject, under the path /msk-policy/ the same as the user DELETE /api/v3/user IAM access key chosen by IAM POST /api/v3/key POST /api/v3/key when the keys table holds no key for the user, DELETE /api/v3/key, DELETE /api/v3/user Default namespace ns- and the last 12 characters of the subject without dashes the same as the user DELETE /api/v3/user Kafka topic <namespace>.<topic>, with 1 partition and replication factor 2 POST /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic} DELETE /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic}, DELETE /api/v3/user Kafka consumer group <namespace>.<group_name> the first consumer that joins it not deleted by the service

The policy lets the IAM user connect to the cluster in MSK_CLUSTER_NAME; read and write the topics whose names start with the user's default namespace and a dot; and use any consumer group and transactional ID on the cluster. With the user's access key, a Kafka client therefore has the permissions to produce to and consume from the user's topics directly, without the service. When IAM_USER_PERMISSIONS_BOUNDARY_ARN is set, the service also sets the policy it names as the user's permissions boundary.

POST /api/v3/key returns the key stored for the user when the keys table holds one, with fresh set to false. Otherwise it creates the user and the default namespace if they are missing, deletes every access key the IAM user holds, creates a new key, stores it, and returns it with fresh set to true. Both answers include endpoint, the value of DEFAULT_SERVERS.

Namespace and topic names are 3 to 32 characters of letters, digits, dashes and underscores, and do not start or end with a dash or an underscore. A namespace is unique across all users. A namespace holds at most MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE topics, 50 by default.

docs.title: The DynamoDB tables
docs.text:
Three environment variables name the tables, and their defaults are the production tables. Every table has one string partition key. When a table does not exist, a write that adds an item, or adds to a set, creates it with on-demand billing; deletes from a missing table are ignored, and reads from it find nothing.

Variable (default) Partition key Items KEYS_TABLE_NAME (diaspora-keys-table) subject One per user that holds a key: access_key, secret_key and create_date of the user's current IAM access key. USERS_TABLE_NAME (diaspora-users-table) subject One per user: namespaces, the set of namespaces the user owns. One more item, with the key __global_namespaces__, holds every namespace any user owns, which keeps namespace names unique. NAMESPACE_TABLE_NAME (diaspora-namespace-table) namespace One per namespace that has had a topic: topics, the set of the namespace's topic names, without the namespace prefix.

Every read is strongly consistent, so a read sees every write made before it. Before a Kafka call, the service checks in these tables that the caller owns the namespace.

docs.title: State in memory
docs.text:
ConsumerService keeps the consumer instances that the consumer routes create. The routes follow the consumer API of the Confluent REST Proxy v2. Each instance holds one KafkaConsumer, connected as the service, and the service finds it by the subject, the namespace, the group name and the instance ID. Only the subject that created an instance can use it. A background thread looks every 30 seconds for instances idle for longer than CONSUMER_INSTANCE_TIMEOUT_MS (5 minutes by default) and closes them. When the process stops, it closes them all.

WebService and NamespaceService each hold a lock. The lock in WebService serializes user and key operations, including the Kafka topic deletes of DELETE /api/v3/user. The lock in NamespaceService serializes only the DynamoDB step of namespace and topic operations: the topic routes call Kafka outside any lock. Both are Python threading locks, so they serialize requests only within one process.

Because of this state, the service runs one worker on one node (Lightsail scale 1). A second worker or node would not hold the consumer instances the first created, so requests for them would get 404 with error code 40403 (Consumer instance not found). Two processes could also run user, key or topic operations on the same records at the same time, since neither would hold the other's locks. Every restart or deploy drops the consumer instances, and clients must create new ones (One worker).

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Changes reach main through pull requests, and a push to main deploys the service to production unless it changes only documentation (What merging does). Report a vulnerability as the security policy says, privately and not in an issue or a pull request.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
Create the virtual environment and install the dev extras as in Running locally, then install the Git hooks:

pre-commit install

To work on the docs, also install the docs extras and build the site. docs.yml runs the same build on every pull request and fails on any warning:

pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs build --strict

To preview the site while you edit, run mkdocs serve --dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8001. It serves the site at http://127.0.0.1:8001/ and rebuilds it on every change. Without --dev-addr it takes port 8000, the port the service uses in Running locally.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
The pre-commit hooks in .pre-commit-config.yaml run on each commit, and pre-commit.ci runs them on every pull request without pushing fixes. To run them on every file:

pre-commit run --all-files

They check whitespace and line endings, large files, merge-conflict markers, the syntax of JSON, YAML and TOML files, the names of test files, spelling (codespell), Python linting and formatting (ruff), types (mypy), the GitHub workflows (actionlint, with shellcheck on their scripts), and committed secrets (detect-secrets). The ruff settings in pyproject.toml ask for lines of at most 79 characters, single quotes, Google-style docstrings, one import per line, and from __future__ import annotations in every module. The mypy settings there ask for type annotations on every function outside the tests.

detect-secrets can flag a value that is not a secret, such as a checksum. Mark such a line with # pragma: allowlist secret in code, and with <!-- pragma: allowlist secret --> in Markdown, where the HTML comment keeps the pragma off the published page.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Testing describes both test sets and how to run them.

  • The unit tests are every test not marked integration. They run on every pull request and before every deploy, with no AWS credentials and with the network blocked: a unit test that opens a network connection fails. Before you open a pull request, run them.
  • The live tests are the tests marked integration. They create real IAM users, DynamoDB items and Kafka topics, and they run only on pushes to main, nightly and by hand, as the live tests' own IAM identity (The live tests' AWS identity). A pull request does not run them. Someone with write access to the repository can run them on a branch with gh workflow run tests.yml --ref <branch>.

Name test files *_test.py. A test that needs AWS or Kafka must be marked with @pytest.mark.integration, or be in one of the modules that tests/conftest.py marks as a whole. A live test that creates an IAM user, a namespace, a topic or a consumer group takes its names from live_subject() or live_namespace() in tests/live_identity, or from the random_subject fixture in tests/conftest.py, which calls live_subject(). The live tests' IAM identity can touch only resources with those names, and the nightly sweep, a script that deletes what live runs leave behind, finds only those (Naming live-test resources).

docs.title: Commits and pull requests
docs.text:
• Branch from main, and name the branch after the kind of change and its subject, such as fix/consistent-reads, ci/split-unit-and-live-tests or docs/deploy-guide-and-runbook. The prefixes in use are feat/, fix/, ci/, docs/ and chore/.
  • Write the commit subject and the pull request title as an imperative sentence that says what changes, such as "Read DynamoDB items with strong consistency".
  • In the pull request description, say what changed and why, and whether merging deploys the service.
  • Pull requests are squash-merged: the title, followed by the pull request number, becomes the subject of the one commit on main.

docs.title: What merging does
docs.text:
A merge is a push to main, which starts these workflows:

  • deployment.yml runs the unit tests and then deploys the service to production, unless every changed file is under docs/, is a Markdown file, or is mkdocs.yml (What triggers a deploy). A deploy restarts the service, which drops every consumer instance.
  • tests.yml runs the unit tests and the live tests.
  • docs.yml builds the docs and publishes them to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This startup script is designed for the Diaspora Admin Console running on the AWS Lightsail instance kafbat-ui at 34.201.83.114. It automates the setup of a Docker environment, installs Docker Compose, and configures a Kafbat UI (v1.5.0) service with essential security and environment settings. Additionally, it establishes a systemd service for managing the Docker Compose application, redirects HTTP traffic from port 80 to port 8080, and schedules an automated reboot every three days.

docs.title: Masked Credentials
docs.text:
The script includes sensitive credentials that have been masked for security purposes:

  • SPRING_SECURITY_USER_NAME: ******** (Web login username)
  • SPRING_SECURITY_USER_PASSWORD: ******** (Web login password)
  • AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ******************** (Used for connecting to MSK)
  • AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: **************************** (Used for connecting to MSK)

docs.title: AWS Lightsail Configuration
docs.text:
To deploy this instance, follow these steps:

  1. Create an Instance:
  2. Navigate to AWS Lightsail.
  3. Choose OS: Linux/Unix → OS only → Ubuntu 24.04 LTS.
  4. Paste the script below into Add launch script, so it initializes and configures the instance.
  5. Allocate at least 1 GB memory and 2 vCPUs for optimal performance.

  6. Set the instance name to kafbat-ui.

  7. Assign a Static IP:

  8. Go to Lightsail → Networking.
  9. Create a static IP in us-east-1, naming it kafbat-ui-static-ip, and attach it to kafbat-ui.

The running instance, created in September 2025, uses Lightsail's WordPress blueprint (Debian 12) instead of Ubuntu, so its login user is bitnami.

docs.title: Startup Script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash

# adapted from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mikegcoleman/todo/master/lightsail-compose.sh
# and https://stackoverflow.com/a/33370375

# Set the front-end for apt to noninteractive to avoid prompts during package installation
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Update package list and perform a dist-upgrade with forced configuration file overwrite
# apt-get update && apt-get -o Dpkg::Options::="--force-confold" dist-upgrade -q -y --force-yes
apt-get update && apt-get -o Dpkg::Options::="--force-confold" dist-upgrade -q -y --allow-downgrades

# Install Docker
curl -sSL https://get.docker.com | sh

# Add the ubuntu user to the docker group
usermod -aG docker ubuntu

# Install Docker Compose
curl -L https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.33.1/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m) -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose

# Create a directory for Docker configuration
mkdir /srv/docker

# Create a Docker Compose configuration file
cat <<EOF > /srv/docker/docker-compose.yml
services:
  kafbat-ui:
    container_name: kafbat-ui
    image: ghcr.io/kafbat/kafka-ui:v1.5.0
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      - DYNAMIC_CONFIG_ENABLED=true
      # Refresh cluster statistics every 5 minutes, not every 30 s (see Broker CPU credits below)
      - KAFKA_UPDATE_METRICS_RATE_MILLIS=300000
      - AUTH_TYPE=LOGIN_FORM
      - SPRING_SECURITY_USER_NAME=******
      - SPRING_SECURITY_USER_PASSWORD=******
      - AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=******
      - AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=******
    volumes:
      - /srv/docker/config.yml:/etc/kafkaui/dynamic_config.yaml
EOF

# Create a Kafka UI configuration file
cat <<EOF > /srv/docker/config.yml
kafka:
  clusters:
    - name: diaspora
      bootstrapServers: b-1-public.diaspora.jdqn8o.c18.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9198,b-2-public.diaspora.jdqn8o.c18.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9198
      properties:
        security.protocol: SASL_SSL
        sasl.mechanism: AWS_MSK_IAM
        sasl.client.callback.handler.class: software.amazon.msk.auth.iam.IAMClientCallbackHandler
        sasl.jaas.config: software.amazon.msk.auth.iam.IAMLoginModule required awsProfileName="default";
EOF

# Download the systemd service file for Docker Compose application
curl -o /etc/systemd/system/docker-compose-app.service https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zahedahmed/todo/master/docker-compose-app.service

# Enable the Docker Compose application service
systemctl enable docker-compose-app

# Start the Docker Compose application in detached mode
docker-compose -f /srv/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d

# Redirect port 80 to port 8080 using iptables
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080

# Install iptables-persistent to save iptables rules
apt-get install -y iptables-persistent
netfilter-persistent save

# Schedule a reboot every 3 days at 4:30 AM
(crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo "30 4 */3 * * /sbin/reboot") | crontab -

docs.title: Upgrading Kafbat UI
docs.text:
The instance runs the image tag pinned in /srv/docker/docker-compose.yml. Docker does not pull a newer image by itself, and the reboot every three days restarts the same image. To move to a new Kafbat UI release:

  1. Connect over SSH as bitnami, from the Lightsail console or with a temporary key from aws lightsail get-instance-access-details --instance-name kafbat-ui --protocol ssh.
  2. Back up the compose file, change the tag on its image: line, then pull and restart: 
    cd /srv/docker
sudo cp -p docker-compose.yml docker-compose.yml.bak
sudoedit docker-compose.yml
sudo docker-compose pull
sudo docker-compose up -d
  3. Check that sudo docker ps shows the new tag and that the login page loads. Kafbat UI takes about two minutes to start on this instance.

To roll back, restore docker-compose.yml.bak and run the last two commands again.

docs.title: Broker CPU credits
docs.text:
The diaspora cluster's brokers are kafka.t3.small instances, which run on CPU credits. Each broker earns 24 credits an hour and holds at most 576; a broker that runs out is throttled to its baseline.

Kafbat UI refreshes its cluster statistics on a timer. Each refresh reads every topic and its configuration, the earliest and latest offsets of every partition, every consumer group and its offsets, and each broker's log directories. In October 2026, with the default refresh of 30 s, the console's load spent broker 1's credits, and topic creation and deletion stalled until the instance was stopped. KAFKA_UPDATE_METRICS_RATE_MILLIS=300000 sets the refresh to 5 minutes, so the topic sizes and consumer lag the console shows can be up to 5 minutes old.

After any change to the console, watch each broker's CPUCreditBalance in CloudWatch (namespace AWS/Kafka, dimensions Cluster Name and Broker ID). If it keeps falling, stop the instance; its static IP keeps the address for the next start.

docs.title: Getting subject and authorization
docs.text:
Every endpoint requires a subject header (your Globus OpenID sub claim) and an authorization header (a Globus OAuth2 Bearer token). The easiest way to obtain both is through the diaspora-event-sdk:

pip install diaspora-event-sdk

from diaspora_event_sdk import Client as GlobusClient

c = GlobusClient()  # triggers Globus login flow on first use

subject = c.subject_openid
authorization = c.web_client.authorizer.get_authorization_header()
namespace = f'ns-{subject.replace("-", "")[-12:]}'

print(f'export SUBJECT="{subject}"')
print(f'export AUTHORIZATION="{authorization}"')
print(f'export NAMESPACE="{namespace}"')

Use these values in the subject and authorization headers when calling the live endpoints below.

docs.title: Try it out
docs.text:
Once you have your subject and authorization, you can interact with the live API directly from the Swagger UI. Click "Try it out" and fill in the header fields on each endpoint.

Alternatively, use curl:

docs.title: User
docs.text:
# Create user
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/user" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

# Delete user
curl -X DELETE "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/user" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

docs.title: Namespace
docs.text:
# List namespaces and topics
curl -X GET "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/namespace" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

docs.title: Topic
docs.text:
# Create topic
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/my-topic" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

# Delete topic
curl -X DELETE "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/my-topic" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

# Recreate topic
curl -X PUT "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/my-topic/recreate" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

A namespace holds at most 50 topics, a limit the service sets with the MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE environment variable. Creating a new topic in a namespace that already holds that many returns "status": "failure" with a message that says to delete a topic first. Once a create adds a topic and leaves the namespace with at least 90% of the limit (45 of 50), the reply appends a warning to message and returns the same sentence in a warning field, which is absent otherwise. At 45 of 50 the warning reads "Namespace my-namespace now holds 45 of 50 topics; a create fails once it holds 50, so delete topics you no longer need." and at 50 of 50 it reads "Namespace my-namespace now holds 50 of 50 topics, the most allowed; delete a topic before you create another." Repeating the create of a topic that already exists, recreating a topic and deleting one are not limited.

docs.title: Consumer
docs.text:
# Create consumer instance
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/consumers/my-group" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"format": "json", "auto.offset.reset": "earliest"}'

# Subscribe to a list of topics (topic patterns are not supported)
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/consumers/my-group/instances/$INSTANCE_ID/subscription" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"topics": ["my-topic"]}'

# Fetch records
curl -X GET "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/consumers/my-group/instances/$INSTANCE_ID/records?timeout=5000" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

# Commit offsets
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/consumers/my-group/instances/$INSTANCE_ID/offsets" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

# Delete consumer instance
curl -X DELETE "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/consumers/my-group/instances/$INSTANCE_ID" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

A consumer instance serves one request at a time. A request that waits more than 10 seconds for another request on the same instance returns 409 with error code 40904; retry it. The fetch timeout is capped at 30000 ms: a larger value waits 30000 ms.
